Circe: Training-Free LLM Self-Evaluation via Component Interaction Consistency

Read cross-layer attention–FFN interaction consistency, representation geometry, and output likelihood to assess a response without reference answers or repeated sampling.

Miao Shuyi

November 5, 2026 ·Preprint ·4-minute read ·Read the paper ·PDF
1Why this matters 2How it works 3What the study finds 4What this means

The short version

A model can confidently repeat an incorrect answer. Circe asks whether the computation behind that answer offers evidence beyond the probability assigned to its words. It measures how attention updates in earlier layers align with attention-induced FFN changes in later layers, then combines that interaction signal with representation geometry and output likelihood.

The evaluator needs one generated response and no additional model training. Its fusion weights are selected on development data; reference answers are not required when scoring a new response. The distinction matters: training-free self-evaluation still needs its calibration and evaluation protocol to be stated clearly.

71.76%Mean AUROC in the component ablation
5 LLMsSix benchmarks across four domains
1 responseNo repeated sampling

Correctness is worth examining in the interaction between components, as well as in the confidence of the final answer.

Why this matters

Hidden-state trajectories aggregate the effects of multiple components. Two answers can have similar output confidence while differing in how attention and feed-forward updates interact. Studying those interactions provides a more specific diagnostic target than aggregate representational drift alone.

How it works

  1. Measure component interaction consistency (CIC): compare earlier attention-update directions with the FFN-output changes induced by attention at later layers.
  2. Compute representation geometry (RG) from normalized displacement and angular changes, and likelihood confidence (LC) from the generated tokens’ mean negative log-likelihood.
  3. Fuse the internal and external signals into a correctness score using development-selected weights, then rank responses without repeated sampling or a reference answer at inference.

What the study finds

The paper evaluates five LLMs on six benchmarks across mathematics, reasoning, knowledge, and understanding. The complete method has the best reported domain-average AUROC, FPR95, and AUPR, and leads AUROC in 18 of 20 model–domain pairs.

In the component ablation, mean AUROC is 71.76%; removing CIC reduces it to 69.71%. Additional evaluations cover 11 languages and a visual geometry task, where the reported AUROC is 71.25%. These are ranking results for response correctness, not task-answering accuracy.

What this means

The central insight is that reliability can depend on how a model coordinates its components, not just on how strongly it prefers its output. Interaction consistency offers a way to inspect that coordination and contributes information that trajectory geometry and likelihood leave out.

This supports computational evidence as an additional axis of model evaluation. Consistency is still a statistical signal rather than a certificate of truth: its usefulness must be checked against task, model, and calibration changes.
